t: LeetCode 2005 — Subtree Removal Game with Fibonacci Tree
o:
## Understanding the problem

order(1) is a single node, and order(n) places a fresh root over order(n−2) (left) and order(n−1) (right), so order(n) contains Fib(n) nodes — astronomically many once n approaches 100. Players alternately pick a node and delete it together with everything below it; whoever is forced to delete the root loses. Deleting the root therefore ends the game as an immediate loss, and the real fight happens among the two Fibonacci subtrees hanging under the root: the player who removes the last non-root node wins, because the opponent must then take the root.

Example walkthrough: for n = 3 the tree is root + order(1) + order(2). Alice deletes the leaf of the order(2) part, leaving two identical single-node subtrees. Whatever Bob removes, Alice removes its twin, and Bob faces the bare root — Alice wins. For n = 1 the only node is the root itself, so Alice loses instantly.

Since materializing Fib(100) nodes is impossible, the solution must come from a game-theory pattern rather than raw simulation.
k: Deleting the global root is always a loss, so play reduces to normal play (last successful remover wins) on the forest under the root.
Two identical copies of any tree form a losing position for the player to move: mirror every move in the twin copy.
order(n−1) can be trimmed into a second copy of order(n−2), handing the opponent exactly such a mirrored position.

a.n: Approach 1: Exhaustive game search on explicit trees (small n)
a.i: Build order(n) explicitly and represent a position as a bitmask of surviving nodes excluding the root. A move clears the deleted node's precomputed subtree mask. A position is winning iff some move reaches a losing position, memoized per mask; the empty mask loses since only the root remains. The state space grows like 2^(Fib(n)), so this is feasible only for tiny n (roughly n <= 6), but it confirms the outcome pattern before you commit to a formula.
s: Recursively construct order(n), recording left/right child ids for every node.
Compute each node subtree mask (its own bit ORed with descendants masks) via post-order traversal.
Memoized win(mask): try deleting every alive non-root node subtree; winning iff any successor loses; empty mask loses.
Return win(full mask minus the root bit).
a.t: O(F · 2^F) where F = Fib(n) nodes — each of 2^F masks tries up to F moves; practical only for very small n

a.i: Call {T, T} — two identical copies of a tree T under the root — a mirrored position. The player to move there loses: reply to any interior deletion by making the identical deletion in the twin, restoring mirrors; if the opponent erases a whole copy instead, you face a lone order(m), which the mover always wins (for m <= 2 delete it outright; otherwise trim its right subtree into a twin pair for the opponent). Alice exploits this on move one: for n >= 4 remove the left branch order(n−3) inside the right subtree order(n−1), leaving twins order(n−2)+order(n−2); for n = 3 delete the lone child of the right subtree (the example's winning move); for n = 2 delete the only child, clearing the forest. Only n = 1 leaves Alice no safe move.
s: Return false when n = 1 — the root is Alice only option.
Otherwise Alice trims the right subtree order(n−1) down to another order(n−2) (or deletes the sole child when n = 2), leaving two equal subtrees under the root.
Mirror every Bob move inside the remaining twin; if he wipes out a whole twin, win the resulting lone order(m) by the same induction.
Conclude: Alice wins exactly when n > 1.
a.t: O(1) — a single comparison once the strategy is established

w:
## Wrap-up

In an interview, run the exhaustive search aloud to discover outcomes (false only for n = 1, true afterwards), then justify the pattern with the mirror argument — the strategy proof impresses more than the final formula. Pitfall: guessing that the outcome follows parity of n fails immediately (n = 3 is odd yet Alice wins). Also remember why deleting a component's top differs from deleting an interior node (the whole component disappears rather than splitting), and that the two subtrees under the root stay independent components throughout. Edge cases: n = 1 and n = 2 deserve explicit mention. Follow-ups: who wins on arbitrary trees (compute Grundy numbers bottom-up), or a variant where taking the root wins the game.
